title: Power of Two
description: Brute force to optimized: dividing by two in a loop versus a single bitwise trick.

blocks.text: Given a number n, decide whether it is a power of two, meaning it can be written as 2 raised to some non-negative whole number exponent, like 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, and so on.

blocks.title: Analogy: Doubling a Single Grain of Rice
blocks.text: Picture starting with exactly one grain of rice and doubling the pile again and again, 1, 2, 4, 8, 16. A power of two is any pile size that could have come from that exact doubling process starting from a single grain, with nothing added or removed along the way. A pile of 6 grains could never appear in this sequence, no matter how many times you double, because doubling alone can never produce it.

blocks.caption: A power of two always has exactly one 1-bit in binary

blocks.content: {"headers":["n","Binary","Power of two?","Why"],"rows":[["16","10000","Yes, exactly one 1-bit","Only one bit is set, matching exactly what pure doubling from a single grain produces."]]}
{"headers":["n","Binary","Power of two?","Why"],"rows":[["6","110","No, two 1-bits","Two bits are set, a shape doubling alone can never produce."]]}

blocks.text: Zero and every negative number are automatically not powers of two, since the definition only ever produces positive results (1, 2, 4, 8, ...). These need to be rejected immediately, before any bit logic runs.
Before writing any code, it helps to reason about what pure doubling actually looks like in binary.

blocks.title: How Should We Think?
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Doubling a single starting unit again and again, 1, 2, 4, 8, always produces a number whose binary form has exactly one bit set, just shifted further left each time.

Observation 2: No combination of doubling steps can ever produce two or more bits set at once, since each doubling only moves the existing single bit, it never creates a second one.

Observation 3: So the entire question "is n a power of two" collapses into a much simpler question: does n have exactly one 1-bit in binary.

Observation 4: Checking for exactly one set bit can be done with a single bitwise trick, no loop over the number's magnitude needed at all.
That reasoning alone already points past the halving loop, straight at a single bitwise check.

The most direct approach is to repeatedly divide n by 2, exactly the same doubling process the analogy describes, but run in reverse. If n ever fails to divide evenly, it could not have come from pure doubling.

items: If n is 0 or negative, return false immediately.
While n is greater than 1, check whether n is even.
If n is odd at this point, it is not a power of two, return false.
Otherwise divide n by 2 and repeat.
If the loop reaches exactly 1, return true.

blocks.caption: Brute force flow: keep halving and check for a clean division every time

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: The n <= 0 check happens before the loop, as a dedicated early rejection, since the loop's own halving logic has no way to naturally reject zero or negative numbers on its own.
The odd check happens before dividing, not after, since dividing an odd number by 2 with integer division would silently discard information needed to catch the failure.
The loop condition is n > 1, not n > 0, specifically so the loop stops exactly when n has been fully reduced to 1 by clean halving, which is the success condition.

blocks.text: This works because a power of two, by definition, can be divided by 2 repeatedly with no remainder until only 1 is left. Any number that hits an odd value above 1 along the way could not have been built purely by doubling.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(log n), since n is halved on every iteration.
Space: O(1), just the number itself being mutated.

Limitation: a power of two has a very recognizable shape in binary, exactly a single 1-bit followed by zeros, like 10000 for 16. Looping and dividing to discover this is unnecessary when that shape can be checked directly with a single bit trick.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why looping and halving works but is not necessary: it rediscovers, one halving at a time, something that is already fully visible in n's binary representation from the start.

What the loop is really checking: whether n has exactly one 1-bit, since only a single-bit number can be halved down to exactly 1 with no remainder at every step.

Can that single-bit shape be tested directly: yes, subtracting 1 from a number with a single 1-bit flips every bit at and below that position.

What happens when the original number is ANDed with that subtracted version: the single 1-bit and all the flipped bits below it never overlap, so the AND is always exactly 0, but only when there was truly just one 1-bit to begin with.

The core idea: compute n AND (n minus 1) directly, no loop, no halving.

A power of two always has exactly one 1-bit in its binary form. Subtracting 1 from a number with a single 1-bit flips every bit below it, including that 1-bit itself, turning it into all 1s below where the original bit was. ANDing the original number with that result always produces zero, but only when there was exactly one 1-bit to begin with.
The optimization is to compute n AND (n minus 1) directly, with no loop at all.
If n is positive, compute n AND (n minus 1). If the result is 0, n had exactly one 1-bit, so it is a power of two.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Value","Binary","Why"],"rows":[["1","n","10000","The starting value, exactly one bit set."],["2","n minus 1","01111","Subtracting 1 clears that single bit and sets every bit below it to 1."],["3","n AND (n minus 1)","00000","The original bit and the newly set bits below never overlap, so the AND is 0."],["4","Result is 0","True, power of two","A zero result only happens when n had exactly one bit to begin with."]]}

blocks.caption: Optimized flow: one bitwise AND replaces the entire loop

blocks.text: This works because subtracting 1 from a number that has a single 1-bit clears that bit and sets every bit below it to 1, while every bit above it stays exactly the same. ANDing the original number, which only has that one bit set above and zeros below, against the subtracted version, which has a zero at that same bit and ones below, can never produce a 1 anywhere, the result is always exactly 0. If n had two or more set bits instead, at least one of those higher bits would survive the AND untouched, giving a non-zero result.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","What Happens","Result"],"rows":[["n has exactly one 1-bit","Subtracting 1 clears it and fills everything below with 1s, which never overlaps with n's own single bit","n AND (n minus 1) equals 0, power of two"],["n has two or more 1-bits","Subtracting 1 only affects the lowest 1-bit and everything below it; at least one higher 1-bit survives untouched in both n and n minus 1","n AND (n minus 1) is non-zero, not a power of two"]]}

items: The n <= 0 check still comes first, exactly as in the brute force, since the bitwise trick alone has no built-in way to reject zero or negative inputs.
n minus 1 is computed once and used directly inside the AND, there is no need to inspect its bits manually, the hardware's own subtraction already produces the correct bit pattern.
Comparing the AND result to 0 is the entire check, no loop, no bit-by-bit inspection required.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(1), a single subtraction and a single AND, regardless of how large n is.
Space: O(1).
10. Further Optimization: Isolating the Lowest Bit

The n AND (n minus 1) trick already runs in O(1), so there is no faster complexity class to reach. There is a closely related bit trick worth knowing as an alternative: n AND (negative n) isolates only the lowest 1-bit of n, using how negative numbers are represented in two's complement. If that isolated lowest bit equals n itself, then n had only that one bit to begin with.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Value","Binary","Why"],"rows":[["1","n","10000","The starting value."],["2","negative n","...10000 (two's complement)","Negating in two's complement flips every bit and adds 1, which leaves the lowest 1-bit position matching n."],["3","n AND (negative n)","10000","Only the lowest 1-bit position survives the AND, every other bit is masked away."],["4","Equals n itself","True, power of two","The isolated lowest bit matching n exactly means n had no other bits set."]]}

blocks.caption: Further optimization: isolate the lowest bit and compare it to n

items: Negation relies on two's complement representation, where negating a number is equivalent to flipping every bit and adding 1, which happens to leave the lowest 1-bit position matching between n and negative n.
n AND (negative n) isolates exactly that lowest 1-bit and zeroes out every other bit, regardless of how many bits n originally had set.

Comparing that isolated bit back to n itself is what distinguishes a true single-bit number, where the isolated bit is the whole number, from a multi-bit number, where the isolated bit is only a small piece of it.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(1), identical to the AND with n minus 1 trick.
Space: O(1). This is a stylistic alternative bit trick, not a complexity improvement over the optimized solution.

blocks.text: The core pattern here is recognizing that a mathematical property, being built purely from doubling, has an exact, checkable shape in binary: a single 1-bit. Once that shape is identified, a single bitwise operation replaces an entire loop.

items: Forgetting to reject n = 0 and negative numbers before applying the bit trick, since the AND trick alone does not naturally exclude them.
Confusing "has a 1-bit" with "has exactly one 1-bit", the trick specifically detects the exactly-one case.
Assuming the loop based brute force is wrong, it is correct, just less efficient than the constant time bit trick.

blocks.text: This is a classic warm up for bit manipulation interviews. Explaining why n AND (n minus 1) clears the lowest 1-bit, rather than just reciting the trick, is what shows real understanding, and it is a building block used again in other problems like counting set bits.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text:
If the interviewer says "can you do this without a loop", think: n AND (n minus 1) equals 0 exactly when n has a single bit set.
If the interviewer says "can you isolate the lowest set bit", think: n AND (negative n), relying on two's complement.
If the interviewer says "what about zero or negative numbers", think: reject them explicitly before applying either bit trick, neither trick excludes them on its own.

items: Can you explain why n AND (n minus 1) always clears exactly the lowest set bit?
Can you use the same n AND (n minus 1) trick to count how many 1-bits n has in total?
How would you check if n is a power of four instead of a power of two?
What is different about how n AND (negative n) behaves compared to n AND (n minus 1)?
Can you solve this using a single expression, with the zero and negative check folded in?
Counting set bits (popcount) problems, which repeatedly apply the exact same n AND (n minus 1) trick to clear one bit at a time.
Any problem checking whether a number has a specific, recognizable shape in binary, a single bit, a contiguous run of bits, alternating bits.
Two's complement tricks in general, isolating the lowest set bit via n AND (negative n) reappears in binary indexed trees and other bit manipulation heavy structures.
Power of four, power of three, and similar "is this a pure power of some base" problems, which often combine a power of two check with an additional constraint.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: The brute force loop runs in O(log n) time and O(1) space. Both bit trick versions run in O(1) time and O(1) space, a genuine complexity class improvement, not just a smaller constant, since the loop disappears entirely.

items: Pattern: a mathematical property, pure doubling, expressed as an exact binary shape, exactly one bit set, checked with a single bitwise trick instead of a loop.
Core Idea: n AND (n minus 1) is 0 exactly when n has a single 1-bit, since subtracting 1 clears that bit and fills everything below with 1s, which can never overlap with a true single bit above it.
Time: O(log n) for the brute force loop, O(1) for both bit trick versions.
Space: O(1) across every version.
Most Important Observation: looping to check for pure doubling and checking for a single 1-bit in binary are two descriptions of the exact same underlying property, and only one of them needs a loop.
Interview Difficulty: easy to get a correct loop based answer, but the constant time bit trick, and explaining why it works, is the expected next step.
One line memory trick: n AND (n minus 1) equals 0 means exactly one bit is set.
